problem.title: Card-fraud scoring service
problem.context: A payments company scores every card transaction for fraud before authorization, processing 3,000 transactions per second normally and up to 15,000 during seasonal sales. Fraud patterns adapt within weeks; confirmed labels arrive days to weeks later. Auditors may ask months later why a transaction was scored as it was. Five data scientists and two ML engineers build the system; operations runs the data centres and shared infrastructure, with no ML platform team.

requirements.text: Score every card transaction before the authorization decision, using the cardholder's recent activity (for example, the spending of the last hour and the last day).
Update the model as new confirmed fraud cases arrive.
For any past score, show which model version and which input values produced it.
During a seasonal peak of 15,000 transactions per second, a score comes back within 30 ms at the 99th percentile.
When the scoring service or one of its data sources fails, authorizations go on. The business accepts weaker fraud detection for up to 15 minutes, but no authorization may fail because of scoring.
An auditor asks about a score from up to 13 months ago. Within one working day the team answers with the model version, the input values and the training data that model was built from.
When the fraud loss rate rises in one segment, a retrained model can be in production within 48 hours, after it has been compared with the current model on recent transactions.
Card data must stay inside the company's PCI-certified environment: no external service may process it.
Seven people build and run the system, with no dedicated ML platform team.

values: Serving: Stateless scoring tier
Feature state: Stream-processed keyed online store
Model rollout: Automated champion challenger with canary
Audit record: Append-only score ledger with immutable model and training snapshots
points.description: A stateless scoring tier receives requests, retrieves keyed online features from the stream-processed store, and scores them with the currently approved model. Automated champion–challenger canaries compare model versions, while the append-only ledger records each score alongside immutable model and training snapshots. Trade-off: This supports horizontal scaling, controlled rollout, and strong auditability, but introduces online-store dependency and feature-read latency. Immutable snapshots and score history also increase storage and operational costs, while automated comparison requires reliable monitoring.

values: Serving: Sharded scoring with colocated state
Feature state: Partitioned stream processor keyed by cardholder
Model rollout: Shadow evaluation then atomic version switch
Audit record: Append-only score ledger with immutable model and training snapshots
points.description: Shards receive scoring requests and colocate each cardholder’s state with a partitioned stream processor, while scores are evaluated against a shadow model before an atomic version switch. Every score is written to an append-only ledger that retains the model and training snapshots used to produce it. Trade-off: This combines low-latency state access, per-cardholder ordering, controlled rollouts, and reproducible audits. It gives up simplicity through shard balancing and state-management concerns, duplicate shadow-evaluation resources, and continually growing immutable storage.

values: Serving: Synchronous scoring from shared relational database
Feature state: Transactional rolling aggregates in database
Model rollout: Manual shadow evaluation then scheduled switch
Audit record: Database score history with retained model artifacts
points.description: Each transaction is scored synchronously using transactional rolling aggregates in a shared relational database, with the active model producing the score. Candidate models are evaluated manually in shadow mode before a scheduled switch, and each score is recorded with retained model artifacts for auditing. Trade-off: This favors transactional consistency, centralized operation, controlled rollout, and reproducibility. It gives up rollout speed and scalability; synchronous database access and aggregate updates can increase latency and database contention.

Trade-off: This provides scalable serving, safer model changes, reproducibility, and degraded availability during outages. It gives up strict feature freshness and fraud-blocking guarantees when caches are stale or fail-open behavior permits authorization, while requiring substantial state, rollout, and audit infrastructure.

points.description: Shards score transactions with colocated state, while a partitioned stream processor keyed by cardholder maintains each cardholder’s features. New models run in shadow, then switch atomically; every score records immutable model and training snapshots, while failures use local last-known features and fail-open authorization. Trade-off: This favors low-latency availability, reproducible audits, and safe model rollout, but fail-open decisions and stale local features can permit more fraud during outages. Colocation and immutable snapshots also increase operational and storage costs.

points.description: The service synchronously reads transactionally maintained rolling aggregates from a shared relational database, scores each authorization request, and records the score with the retained model artifact. New models are evaluated manually in shadow mode before a scheduled switch; if scoring is unavailable, cached aggregates support a fail-open authorization fallback. Trade-off: This favors consistency, traceability, and controlled rollout. It gives up resilience and potentially fraud-prevention strength during outages, because synchronous database dependence and fail-open behavior can permit transactions without a fresh score.

values: Serving: Embedded model in authorization service
Feature state: Replicated in-memory rolling aggregates
Model rollout: Signed model bundles staged to each shard
Audit record: Append-only score ledger with immutable model and training snapshots
Failure handling: Cached aggregates and fail-open authorization fallback
points.description: Each authorization shard runs the embedded model against replicated in-memory rolling aggregates, while signed model bundles are staged to shards for controlled updates. For every decision, the service appends a score record referencing immutable model and training snapshots; if aggregate state or scoring dependencies fail, it uses cached aggregates and fails open, allowing authorization to proceed. Trade-off: This favors low-latency, locally available scoring and strong provenance, but replication and staging add memory, distribution, and rollout-coordination costs. Fail-open behavior and cached or stale aggregates preserve availability but can reduce fraud-detection accuracy and permit fraudulent transactions during failures.

points.description: The stateless scoring tier retrieves keyed, stream-maintained features from the online store and scores requests using the current champion or canary model. It records each score with immutable model and training snapshots, while a local feature cache and circuit breaker enable a fail-open authorization fallback during dependency failures. Trade-off: This supports horizontal scaling, controlled rollouts, reproducible audits, and continued authorization availability. It gives up some protection during outages because fail-open decisions may approve fraudulent transactions, and cache staleness can reduce scoring accuracy.

Trade-off: This favors auditable, controlled model changes and continued authorization during failures, but accepts cache staleness, replica lag, database dependence, slower rollouts, and the fraud exposure of fail-open decisions.

points.description: Each authorization shard runs the embedded model against replicated in-memory rolling aggregates, rebuilding them through event replay and using signed model bundles staged locally. It appends scores with immutable model and training snapshots, while health checks determine whether to use cached aggregates or fail open when scoring dependencies are unhealthy. Trade-off: This provides low-latency, shard-local decisions, reproducibility, and strong auditability, but duplicates state and requires replay, bundle distribution, and ledger storage. It also accepts increased fraud exposure during health-gated fail-open periods and possible aggregate staleness.

approaches.idea: What if a stateless scoring tier reads stream-maintained online features and automates champion/challenger rollout?
What if scoring and keyed feature state are colocated by cardholder, with shadow validation before model switch?
What if a shared relational database owns rolling aggregates, score history and the synchronous scoring path?
What if the authorization service embeds the model and keeps replicated rolling state on each shard?

trajectory.observation: Recent keyed features and versioned score lineage are represented directly, but no failure fallback is present. The numeric latency target and 48-hour retrain cycle need measurement; several moving services add work for the small team.

adrs.title: Where scoring and recent activity state run
adrs.context: The service must use current cardholder activity before authorization at seasonal peak, remain available during component failure, and keep card data within the PCI environment. A local path reduces hops but increases state ownership; shared services reduce duplication but can add latency and failure concentration.
